A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network fell back to DONE at once (training episode length went to 1.0, with zero placements on dev). The traces show why. The observed target is the design cyclically shifted by X/2 = 4 columns along x: row 2 is "03320000" in the design and "00000332" in the observation, and row 0 of design 2 is "00100011" against "00110010". Rows are not shifted. Actions and rewards use the design's coordinates; for example, the 1x2 placed at row 7, columns 6-7 earned -0.010, meaning one cell inside the target and one outside. The starting network only uses local 3x3 convolutions, so it cannot line the target up with where actions land. Every placement looks like a penalty, and DONE (reward 0) wins. I don't know whether the build channels are shifted too. So each candidate gives the first learned layer both the original and the shifted copies of the observation, built only by slicing and concatenating, and lets that layer choose. These are the first results, so the 0.000 baseline gives no noise figure yet.

### Round 2
The target channels appear rolled by X/2 columns relative to the build (the trace shows the design shifted by 4 columns), and the starting network collapsed to DONE because of it. Adding a half-roll copy of the input fixed this: r1c1 scored 0.59. Concatenating every roll also worked but was worse (0.44), so extra inputs hurt. More PPO updates (n_envs 128, 16 minibatches) with gamma 0.97 gave the best result, 0.82. Both of its seeds (0.79 and 0.85) are above both seeds of r1c1, so the gain looks real. Training success was still rising at the end (0.69 to 0.73), so the agent is limited by its training budget, not by the network's capacity. Runs take about 70 s, far below the time limit. This round: push the update count further, trade PPO epochs for more samples, and test one cheap change to the network (feeding global context back to each cell's placement logits).

### Round 3
The target channels are observed shifted cyclically by X//2 columns. Adding a half-rolled copy of the observation fixed this, taking dev success from 0 to 0.59. After that, the recipe gave the biggest gains. More PPO updates helped twice in a row: 0.59, then 0.82 (n_envs 128), then 0.885 (n_envs 64, r2c1, the current best). Training success was still rising at the end of every run, so updates or sample efficiency look like the main limit, not network capacity. Two epochs with more samples gave one excellent seed (0.90) and one collapsed seed (0.15), so it is unstable. Broadcasting the global vector to every cell gave 0.857 against 0.82 on the same recipe. That gain is small but within plausible signal, and adds almost no compute. Bigger networks would cost samples while training is still improving, so this round tests: broadcast on top of the best recipe, about 2x more updates, and a higher learning rate.

### Round 4
The observed target is shifted by X//2 columns. Adding a half-rolled copy of the observation fixed this: the score went from 0 to 0.59. After that, the recipe mattered most. Refreshing data more often at the same number of gradient steps (128→64 envs, 128 samples per minibatch) raised dev success from 0.82 to 0.885, and lr 2e-3 raised it to 0.913 (best; both seeds about 0.90 or higher). Going further failed. Rollout_len 8 collapsed (0.076), probably from heavy bootstrapping and tiny advantage batches. Two epochs with 128 envs lost one seed (0.90 vs 0.15). The global broadcast gave no clear gain (0.874 vs 0.885). At the end of training, training success (0.90) roughly equals dev success, so the limit is how fast the agent learns, not generalisation or capacity. A bigger network would cost samples and updates. For this last round I keep the best architecture and change one optimisation setting per candidate: a higher lr, 3 PPO epochs (about 30% more fresh samples and updates), and a lower entropy bonus so the greedy policy sharpens sooner.

## Trial it ended with
name: half-roll, 4x updates, lr 2e-3
hypothesis: Same as r2c1, but lr goes from 0.001 to 0.002. With only about 120 updates and training success still rising at the end, a bigger step size should get further within the budget. PPO clipping and gradient clipping should limit instability. Refuted if dev success falls below about 0.86, or one seed collapses, which would mean the bottleneck is update count rather than step size.
